title: Bandwidth-prioritized KV residency probe
body:
Summary:
This note captures an exploratory investigation into eviction scoring that incorporates observed memory bandwidth pressure and page-level residency costs. The hypothesis: current LRU-ish heuristics over-prioritize recency and miss opportunity to avoid high-latency page fetches when memory channels or DMA engines are saturated. By biasing residency scores using per-page or per-resident-region bandwidth impact estimates we can reduce paging-induced tail latency for mixed-length and multi-tenant workloads with minimal impact to cache hit-rate.

Background:
- Problem observed: under mixed short/long sequence traffic and model switching, we see tail-latency spikes correlated with increased GPU memcpy contention and host DRAM read amplification (paging). Existing eviction heuristics evict entries that are "least recently used" without regard for the cost of re-populating that entry (e.g., page faults, number of memory pages that must be read, DMA stalls).
- Practical constraints: We need a scoring approach that is cheap to compute in the hot path, compatible with our continuous-batching runtime, and incremental (no global sorts).

Approach overview:
1) Instrumentation to estimate "bandwidth impact" per resident entry: approximate number of host memory pages pinned by that entry, and recent bytes transferred by those pages over a sliding window.
2) Residency score = alpha * recency_score + beta * reuse_rate - gamma * bandwidth_impact (alpha/beta/gamma tunable). Lower score => candidate for eviction.
3) Soft-priority eviction: avoid evicting entries with high bandwidth_impact during periods of channel saturation; instead evict several lower-impact entries to free space.

Experiments run:
- Setup: 8x A100 (or equivalent internal cluster emulation), multi-tenant synthetic load: 60% short-chat (seq_len 128), 40% long-generation (seq_len 2048) with bursts. Cache capacity tuned to 60% of working set so eviction occurs.
- Baselines: current LRU-like eviction (production), naive size-aware eviction (evict largest entries first), and our bandwidth-prioritized scorer (BP-scorer).
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 latency for token generation, cache hit-rate, page-faults/sec, DRAM read bandwidth, GPU memcpy wait time, and number of DMA stalls per minute.

Key results (summary):
- Under sustained medium load (QPS ~ 250 per GPU): BP-scorer reduced p99 token latency by ~18% vs LRU, with a 3 percentage-point drop in raw cache hit-rate.
- During burst periods (sudden long-seq ramp): BP-scorer reduced page-faults/sec by ~40% and observed DRAM read bandwidth peaks were ~22% lower.
- Observed side-effect: slightly higher p50 for short-chat traffic (about +6%); tradeoff seems acceptable for latency SLO-driven workloads.

Profiling notes and evidence:
- Flamegraphs of memcpy time show fewer long-duration host->GPU memcpy calls during BP-scorer runs.
- Perf counters on host show reduced last-level-cache (LLC) misses when eviction avoided high-page-count entries.
- Telemetry trace samples indicate fewer multi-page page-fault sequences (page-in batches), which previously serialized downstream processing and caused token-level stalls.

Implementation details (prototype):
- Bandwidth estimator: lightweight per-entry counters updated on page-populate events and sampled bytes copied by the page_mapper. We kept counters as 16-bit saturating ints and decay them with a 1s half-life for stability.
- Scoring update path: updated at access-time only (no global scans) — when an entry is touched we update its recency_ts and increment reuse counters; we periodically (every 200ms) do a local eviction pass that picks candidates by scanning a shard and computing the score.
- Saturation detector: separate signal that reports when DRAM read bandwidth or GPU memcpy queue length crosses thresholds. When saturated, we increase gamma dynamically to prefer avoiding high-bandwidth-impact evictions.

Observations and design tradeoffs:
- Accuracy vs cost: fine-grained per-page accounting is costly. Our sampling approach (count page-in batches and bytes moved) seems to hit a good sweet spot.
- Multi-tenancy fairness: entries from noisy tenants sometimes have inflated bandwidth scores; we introduced a tenant-normalization factor so heavy tenants don't lock cache capacity indefinitely.
- Cold-start behavior: initial traffic after model load still causes page-in spikes. We added a short grace window where newly-addded entries have reduced bandwidth penalty to allow their initial warmup.

Open questions:
- Should the bandwidth-impact be absolute (bytes) or normalized by entry size? Our experiments used absolute bytes; size-normalized seemed to bias too much towards tiny high-cost entries.
- Interaction with KV prefetch: prefetching wide contexts might increase bandwidth-impact and change ordering; need to simulate prefetch + BP-scorer together.
- Long-term stability: will tenants gaming the system (small writes, repeated touching) inflate reuse and evade eviction? Consider integrating token-level cost accounting or request-pricing signals.

Next steps / action items:
- Run a larger-scale cluster test with real production traffic replay for 72 hours (owner: Michael Chen, JIRA SRV-8421).
- Add a canary in Dedicated to test tenant normalization and tune gamma dynamics (owner: Luis Ortega).
- Add more granular telemetry: per-page residency distribution and correlation to memcpy latency (owner: Ananya Rao).
- Draft runbook entry describing when to increase gamma and how to debug DRAM/gpu memcpy bottlenecks (owner: eng-sre).

Appendix: quick commands and links
- Local repro: tools/repro/run_kv_bandwidth_probe.sh --config configs/bp_probe_small.yaml
- Perf commands used: sudo perf record -a -g -F 99 -- sleep 60; perf script | FlameGraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl | FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl > memcpy-bp.svg
- Related PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2190 (prototype scoring + metrics)

Notes to self (short):
- Keep scoring cheap. Avoid per-request per-page loops in hot path.
- Watch out for counter wrap-around in the per-entry estimator (use saturating arithmetic).
- Validate on both NVDIMM and standard DRAM hosts; behavior differs significantly.

If useful, I can extract a minimal patch for the scorer and run with the built-in traffic generator on Tuesday.
